messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Linh Tran is a 74-year-old Vietnamese American woman, married for over four decades, who works as a software engineer at a mid-sized technology firm where she has spent the better part of her professional life. She came to the clinic in a state of quiet exhaustion, choosing her words carefully, as though she had rehearsed how little she needed to say.

Fourteen months ago, Linh's youngest grandchild, a three-year-old boy named Minh, was rushed to the emergency room after a sudden respiratory collapse at Linh's home, where she had been babysitting him alone. She had been in the kitchen when the house went completely silent — the ordinary background noise of a toddler playing had simply stopped. By the time she reached the living room, Minh was unresponsive on the floor. The ambulance ride, the fluorescent corridors, the sharp smell of antiseptic that met her as she was ushered through the hospital doors, the sounds of monitors and the squeal of wheels on linoleum — all of it compressed into a period of hours during which she was told, more than once, that her grandson might not survive. He did survive, after several days in intensive care, and he has since recovered fully. Linh has not.

In the weeks following Minh's hospitalization, Linh began to notice that certain moments pulled her back into that afternoon with a force she could not resist. Driving to work, the sound of a car engine idling or accelerating at a particular pitch would arrive in her chest before it arrived in her mind, and she would find herself gripping the steering wheel with the same helpless urgency she had felt waiting for the ambulance. Walking through the office building, the faint antiseptic smell from the cleaning crew's morning rounds could stop her mid-stride, flooding her with terror so complete that she would have to stand still and wait for it to pass. Most disorienting of all was silence. At home, if her husband stepped out and the house fell quiet, or at the office when the open-plan floor emptied during lunch, the absence of sound became something almost physical — she had come to believe, with a certainty she could not argue herself out of, that silence meant something terrible was already happening just out of her sight.

Linh works in a building where the cleaning staff use hospital-grade disinfectant on the shared surfaces each morning. She arrives early, as she always has, but now she lingers in the parking garage, timing her entrance to avoid the smell in the corridors. She has rearranged her schedule so that she attends fewer in-person meetings, telling colleagues she is managing her workload more efficiently from her desk. Her manager has noticed that she is less available than she once was, and a recent performance review mentioned her reduced collaboration. Linh did not explain.

At night, she lies awake long after her husband has fallen asleep, listening. She would not describe it as anxiety exactly — she would say she simply cannot afford not to listen. When memories of Minh on the floor surface, they do not arrive as images so much as a wave of feeling that is indistinguishable from the original terror, and sometimes the terror comes without any image at all, without any clear reason she can name, and that formlessness frightens her almost more than the memories themselves.

What frightens her most, in the way that keeps her awake, is the conviction that she is responsible. She had been in the kitchen. She had been distracted. She had not checked on him soon enough. She has turned this sequence over so many times that it has become a kind of verdict rather than a question. She is also certain that the world does not offer the protections she once assumed it did, and that no amount of vigilance on her part can guarantee that the people she loves will remain safe — a belief that coexists, painfully, with her inability to stop trying.

It was her husband who finally persuaded her to seek help, after she woke him for the third consecutive night, sitting upright and listening to silence. She came to the clinic hoping, she said softly, to be able to sit in a quiet room without being afraid.
